overview.title: 📖 Overview: Opening Tractate Shabbat With Carrying
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 2a–2b
overview.hebrewSource: יְצִיאוֹת הַשַּׁבָּת, שְׁתַּיִם שֶׁהֵן אַרְבַּע בִּפְנִים, וּשְׁתַּיִם שֶׁהֵן אַרְבַּע בַּחוּץ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Tractate Shabbat opens not with a general statement of the Shabbat prohibitions but with the specific, technical melakha of carrying between the private and public domains. The mishna pictures a poor person standing outside and a homeowner standing inside, and works through eight scenarios of handing objects across the boundary, sorting out who is liable and who is exempt. The Gemara immediately compares this mishna's phrasing to nearly identical language used elsewhere in the Mishna — about oaths, about impurity, about leprosy signs — to ask why our mishna adds the extra detail of 'inside' and 'outside.' It resolves this with Rav Pappa's distinction between liability and exemption, then investigates whether the term for 'carrying out' also covers carrying in, and closes with a numbers puzzle about how many distinct actions the mishna is really describing.

slides.title: 🚪 The Mishna's Eight Cases
slides.subtitle: A poor person outside, a homeowner inside — who completes the act decides who is liable
rows: Poor person extends his hand in and places an object in the homeowner's hand, or takes one from it and pulls out
Poor person alone performs the complete act of carrying
Homeowner extends his hand out and places an object in the poor person's hand, or takes one from it and pulls in
Homeowner alone performs the complete act of carrying
Poor person extends his hand in; homeowner takes from it, or places into it and the poor person pulls out
The act is split between two people
Homeowner extends his hand out; poor person takes from it, or places into it and the homeowner pulls in
The act is split between two people

callout.label: Key point:
callout.text: The Torah prohibition of carrying requires one person to perform the whole act — lifting from one domain and placing in the other. Whenever the act is divided between two participants, neither has completed a full melakha, so both are exempt by Torah law.

slides.title: 🔍 Why Spell Out 'Inside and Outside' Here?
slides.subtitle: Shevuot's parallel mishna just says 'two that are four' and stops

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: We learned in tractate Shevuot: oaths that render one liable to a sin-offering are also 'two that comprise four.' Why does our mishna add 'inside' and 'outside,' when the mishna in Shevuot teaches 'two that are four' and nothing more?

lines.speaker: First answer
lines.text: Here, in Shabbat, the primary discussion of these halakhot, the tanna teaches both the primary categories of labor (אָבוֹת) and their subcategories (תּוֹלָדוֹת). There, in Shevuot, only the primary categories are taught.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But the primary categories are just the two acts of carrying out! Where does Shevuot's count of four come from?

lines.speaker: Rav Pappa
lines.text: Rather: here the tanna teaches cases of liability and cases of exemption. There, in Shevuot, only cases of liability are taught, and nothing else.

callout.label: Parallel structure:
callout.text: The Gemara measures this against two other 'two that are four' teachings — awareness of impurity before and after eating sacred food or entering the Temple, and the two-plus-two shades of leprosy signs, baheret and se'et and their lighter derivatives.

slides.title: 🔄 Does 'Carrying Out' Include Carrying In?
slides.subtitle: The mishna in Shevuot only says יְצִיאוֹת — 'acts of carrying out'

steps.content: 1️⃣ Objection: Shevuot's mishna speaks of יְצִיאוֹת, 'carrying out.' Yet its four cases must include carrying IN too, or there is no way to reach four

2️⃣ Rav Ashi: The tanna in Shevuot also calls carrying in by the name 'carrying out' — proven from a mishna that calls one who transfers an object 'from domain to domain' liable, which plainly includes carrying into the private domain
3️⃣ Reason: any act of lifting an object from its place and moving it to another domain is called הוֹצָאָה, 'carrying out' — the term is general, not literal
4️⃣ Ravina: our own mishna proves it precisely — it opens with 'acts of carrying out' (יְצִיאוֹת), yet its very first case is the poor person handing an object into the homeowner's hand

callout.label: Alternative:
callout.text: Rava offers a different fix entirely: read the word not as רְשׁוּיוֹת יְצִיאוֹת ('acts of carrying out') but as רְשׁוּיוֹת ('domains') — 'the domains of Shabbat are two that comprise four' — removing the difficulty altogether.

slides.title: ⚖️ 'Two That Are Four' — Three Parallel Teachings
slides.subtitle: The Gemara reads our mishna against two other mishnayot using the identical formula

boxes.title: Shabbat: Carrying
items: Two basic acts (carrying out from private to public, or public to private)
×2 for inside/outside = four cases each, eight total
Includes BOTH liability and exemption cases

boxes.title: Shevuot: Oaths
items: Swearing to do / not to do an act in the future (from the Torah)
Swearing that one did / did not do it in the past (added by amplification)

boxes.title: Tumah & Nega'im
items: Awareness of impurity: forgetting before, or forgetting after, eating sacred food or entering the Temple
Leprosy signs: baheret and se'et, each with a lighter derivative shade
Both cited as models for 'two that are four'

callout.label: Method:
callout.text: The Gemara assumes a shared formula must mean a shared structure — until it finds, case by case, where the parallel breaks down.

slides.title: 🔢 Rav Mattana's Count: Eight, Twelve, or Sixteen?
slides.subtitle: A closing puzzle about how many actions the mishna truly describes

nodes.content: ❓ Rav Mattana to Abaye: the mishna's second half lists four cases where 'both are exempt' — but each involves TWO people acting together. Isn't that eight actions, for a total of twelve, not eight?
🤨 Abaye: by that reasoning, even the mishna's FIRST half — its four straightforward liability cases — involves both a giver and a receiver. That would make sixteen actions!
💬 Rav Mattana: 'That is not difficult — granted...' — the daf breaks off mid-answer, to be resumed on 3a

callout.label: To be continued:
callout.text: Daf 2b ends on a cliffhanger; the resolution of Rav Mattana's count opens the next daf.

summary.principle: The prohibition of carrying on Shabbat requires one person to complete both the lifting and the placing; the Gemara's term 'carrying out' is general enough to include carrying in, and Shabbat's mishna, unlike Shevuot's, records both liability and exemption.

flowSteps.content: 🚪 Mishna: 2 basic transfer-acts × inside/outside = 8 cases (4 liable, 4 exempt)
❓ Why does Shabbat's mishna add 'inside/outside' where Shevuot's parallel mishna omits it?
⚖️ Rav Pappa: Shabbat teaches liability AND exemption; Shevuot teaches only liability

columns.content: 🔄 'Carrying out' is a general term that covers carrying IN too (Rav Ashi, Ravina)
🔢 Rav Mattana vs. Abaye: are there really 8, 12, or 16 distinct actions?

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: liability for carrying requires ONE person to complete both lifting and placing — splitting the act exempts everyone involved

quiz.q: In the mishna's first case, the poor person extends his hand into the private domain and places an object into the homeowner's hand. Who is liable?
o: The homeowner alone
The poor person alone
Both of them
Neither of them
quiz.e: The poor person performed the complete act of carrying — both lifting and placing — so he alone is liable; the homeowner, who did nothing, is exempt.

quiz.q: Why are both the poor person and the homeowner exempt in the cases where one extends a hand and the other takes or places the object?
o: Because carrying on Shabbat is never prohibited
Because the prohibited labor of carrying requires one person to perform the entire act of lifting and placing
Because only homeowners can be held liable
Because the object was too small to count
quiz.e: When the act is divided between two people, neither one performed the complete melakha, so by Torah law both are exempt.

quiz.q: According to Rav Pappa, what actually distinguishes how the mishna in Shabbat teaches 'two that are four' from how the mishna in Shevuot teaches it?
o: Shabbat's mishna is about impurity, Shevuot's is about labor
Shabbat's mishna teaches only exemption cases, Shevuot's teaches only liability cases
Shabbat's mishna teaches both liability and exemption cases; Shevuot's teaches only liability cases
There is no real difference between them
quiz.e: Rav Pappa resolves the difficulty by saying Shabbat's mishna, being the primary discussion of these halakhot, records both liable and exempt scenarios, while Shevuot's mishna records only the liable ones.

quiz.q: What proof does Ravina bring that the term 'acts of carrying out' (יְצִיאוֹת) also covers carrying in?
o: A verse from the Torah about Shabbat
The mishna's own structure: it opens with 'acts of carrying out,' yet its very first case is the poor person carrying an object INTO the homeowner's hand
A ruling of Rabban Gamliel
The fact that priests eat teruma at night
quiz.e: Ravina points out that our mishna is precise: right after using the heading 'carrying out,' its first example describes carrying in, proving the term covers both directions.

quiz.q: What is the substance of Rav Mattana's challenge to Abaye about the mishna's count of cases?
o: That there should be only four cases, not eight
That the mishna's second half, where 'both are exempt,' involves two people's actions each, so the true count should be twelve, not eight
That the poor person should always be liable
That the mishna never mentions a homeowner
quiz.e: Rav Mattana notes that in the four 'both exempt' cases, two separate individual actions occur (one lifts, another places), which by his count would bring the total to twelve rather than eight.
